title: Why the Quran?
subtitle: A cumulative case from message, form, transmission, historical setting, and lived guidance
summary: The Quran's claim to be revelation cannot be proved by quoting its self-description alone. Its case is cumulative: a sustained account of God and humanity, a distinctive Arabic proclamation, early and unusually stable transmission, a historically consequential prophetic setting, and a form of guidance meant to be recited and lived. Each line of evidence has limits and alternatives that deserve direct examination.

sections.title: Understanding Why the Quran?
sections.body: The Quran's claim to revelation is cumulative. It includes its account of God and humanity, Arabic form, early transmission, Muhammad's setting, and lived guidance. Each line has limits and alternatives that deserve examination.

sections.title: What Would Count as Evidence?
sections.body: The Quran calls itself guidance from God. That states its claim but does not prove it alone. A fair inquiry compares revelation with authorship, borrowing, sincere experience, political construction, and later development. No feature settles the question by itself. The case joins the Quran's view of God, moral vision, form, setting, transmission, and role in worship.

sections.title: The Message at Its Center
sections.body: Across law, story, devotion, and argument, the Quran returns to Tawhid: the incomparable Creator alone deserves worship. People are dependent yet responsible, forgetful yet able to repent. Prophets share one call; power is a trust; care for the vulnerable is worship. Quran 4:82 asks whether serious inconsistency would be expected from a human source. A surface tension is not automatically a contradiction.

sections.title: Arabic Form and the Challenge of Inimitability
sections.body: The Quran is recited Arabic discourse. Its sound, rhythm, imagery, argument, and structure do not fit ordinary poetry or prose. Quran 17:88 challenges humans and jinn to produce its like. Literary judgment needs language skill, and criteria remain debated. Translation gives access to the message; Arabic is needed for detailed form.

sections.title: A Text Available for Examination
sections.body: The Quran was transmitted through recitation and written copies. Early manuscripts, the Uthmanic consonantal text, prayer, memorization, and named readings support early stability. Early script did not mark every vowel. Canonical *qira'at* preserve limited differences within the early consonantal skeleton. Quran 15:9 gives the divine claim; history supplies evidence but cannot measure providence.

sections.title: Muhammad and the Quran's Emergence
sections.body: The Quran addresses opposition in Mecca, migration, community life, conflict, family, treaties, worship, and public ethics. It sometimes corrects Muhammad and preserves difficult moments. Its worship is directed beyond him to God. Historians examine Jewish, Christian, Arabian, and late-antique ideas, oral culture, politics, and later sources. Similarity can reflect shared inheritance or borrowing; Muslim belief explains both continuity and correction.

sections.title: Historical and Predictive Claims
sections.body: Some arguments appeal to history, prophecy, or knowledge said to be unavailable to Muhammad. Quran 30:2-4 says defeated Romans would prevail within a few years. Evaluation needs the date, Arabic time expression, event sequence, and early evidence. Scientific-miracle claims need caution. Broad language should not be retrofitted into later discoveries. The Quran's main appeal is its signs, message, form, and call to reflection.

sections.title: A Book Recited and Lived
sections.body: The Quran shapes prayer, remembrance, fasting, charity, family ethics, grief, repentance, and justice. Generations memorize and recite it across cultures. Transformative power matters but is not conclusive. The test is the character it calls for: humility before God, truthfulness, patience, generosity, justice, and hope.

sections.title: How to Reach a Responsible Verdict
sections.body: Read complete surahs in more than one respected translation. Use commentary for Arabic and early interpretation, then consult academic work that does not assume revelation. Study manuscripts and readings without slogans. For Muslims, the convergence points to God's final preserved revelation. Historical method cannot certify divine authorship alone. Quran 2:2 calls the book guidance.

sections.title: Key Takeaways: Why the Quran?
sections.body: The Quran's message, transmission, form, and call to worship one God deserve sustained study. The invitation to Islam rests on honest examination, not one isolated feature. Sincere prayer for guidance can accompany that search. The purpose is truth, not victory over another faith.

faq.question: Does preservation prove that the Quran is from God?
faq.answer: No. Preservation makes the text available for study. Divine origin also requires its message, form, messenger, context, and rival explanations.

faq.question: Are all Quran copies letter-for-letter identical?
faq.answer: Copies within one reading are highly standardized. Canonical readings preserve limited differences in sounds and wording from early transmission. Muslim scholarship treats them as authorized.

faq.question: Can someone who does not know Arabic assess the Quran?
faq.answer: Yes, with limits. Translations convey much of the message. Precise wording, sound, and rhetoric need Arabic study.

faq.question: Is the Quran's challenge to imitate it a scientific test?
faq.answer: No. It is a literary and theological challenge. Its force can be argued, but it is not a laboratory measurement.

faq.question: Where should a first-time reader begin?
faq.answer: Read several complete shorter surahs, then connected passages such as Maryam, Yusuf, or al-Baqarah. Use a reliable translation and responsible commentary.

faq.question: How Should the Quran Be Evaluated?
faq.answer: Read the Quran in a reliable translation. Assess its message, form, setting, transmission, and rival explanations. A cumulative case should not treat one feature as conclusive.
